paper_title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward--reverse consistency force that joint positive--negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting), which aggregates each prompt's rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain hidden forwardreverse consistency force that joint positivenegative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting), which aggregates each prompts rewards into shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards. sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Visual diffusion and flow-matching models1 are typically trained to fit the data distribution by regressing noise or velocity targets rather than to optimize downstream criteria such as visual quality, motion quality, or human preference, making reward-guided fine-tuning central to recent image and video generation tasks [2,3]. We focus on online diffusion Reinforcement Learning (RL), which, unlike differentiable reward-model optimization such as ReFL [4] or offline preference learning such as Diffusion-DPO [5], evaluates clean samples from the evolving generator and can use black-box rewards. Because these rewards arrive only after complete output is generated, online diffusion RL faces credit-assignment problem: costly output-level feedback must be translated into effective updates across many denoising states [6,7]. Within this paradigm, reverse-process RL [8], such as Flow-GRPO and its variants [6,9,10,11], optimizes sampled denoising transitions via group-based endpoint reward feedback. It trains on states actually visited by the generator but requires ODE-to-SDE conversion for tractable likelihoods, and its policy gradient updates each selected transition along its own transition-level sampling noise, weighted by trajectory-level advantage that this transition only partly determines, resulting in poor credit assignment and limiting training efficiency. Forward-process RL, such as DiffusionNFT [7], instead applies forward noising to the generated clean samples and regresses velocities with reward-weighted positive and negative objectives. It needs no transition likelihoods and is highly efficient, but it is unstable without two stabilizers: joint positivenegative training and an exponential moving average (EMA) rollout policy whose lag must be tuned for each task [7]. Neither family is thus both efficient and stable without per-task tuning. In this paper, we focus on studying the instability of forward-process RL and developing scalable algorithm which is both stable and efficient. We first examine NFT-style training, starting from puzzle: its positive and negative branches share the same ideal reward-improving direction, so either alone should suffice, yet each alone collapses (Figure 2(a)). We find that NFTs targets, built from forward-noised endpoints, implicitly assume that the models sampling velocity equals the ideal forward velocity induced by its own endpoints. The two differ in practice, and the gap introduces hidden non-reward-improving forwardreverse consistency force: the positive branch pulls each states velocity toward the ideal forward velocity and the negative branch pushes it away. Joint training can cancel this force but only partially, since reward centering balances rewards across samples rather than at each state. The residual can destabilize training and slow the reward optimization. We further show that EMA stabilizes NFT through the restoration force of its lagged reference, not through off-policy rollouts, but the EMA trick must be tuned per task. Driven by these insights, we introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting). It borrows supervised velocity regression from forward-process training but applies updates to states and actions during reverse-process rollouts. It first aggregates each prompts samples and rewards into shared reward-improving direction G(c), then regresses each visited states action toward its guided target (Section 4.1). As this target never involves the forward velocity, the consistency force is removed by construction rather than by cross-sample cancellation, and each state receives an explicit reward-improving direction instead of scalar advantage passed through likelihood ratios. second update with trust-region mask mechanism on each rollout adds restoration force proportional to each states drift, replacing EMA with no schedule to tune (Section 4.2). We summarize our main contributions as follows: Main Contributions 1. Diagnosing the instability of NFT-style training. The NFT objective implicitly contains harmful forwardreverse consistency force that joint training cancels only partially (Section 3.1). 2. Identifying restoration as the key stabilizer. EMA stabilizes NFT through restoration rather than off-policy data, but requires per-task tuning (Section 3.2). 3. Aggregation-first reward tilting with adaptive restoration. DiffusionART removes the consistency force by construction, eliminating the need for EMA with drift-adaptive restoration (Section 4). 4. Efficient and stable training. DiffusionART matches the strongest baselines efficiency on SD3.5-M without EMA or per-task tuning. Under VQ:MQ = 1:1 weights on HunyuanVideo-13B, it reaches the late-stage mean VQ and MQ rewards of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 fewer GPU hours, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards, respectively. For image-to-video generation, it reaches MQ 6 with 4.8 fewer GPU hours than Flow-GRPO-Fast (Section 5). 1We use diffusion as general term. Our paper targets rectified-flow with linear datanoise interpolation [1], which shares the core principles of diffusion.

sections.content: DiffusionNFT is highly efficient, but its stability relies on joint positivenegative training and an off-policy EMA rollout policy [7]. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We study the efficiency, stability, and scalability of DiffusionART, progressing from text-to-image (T2I) generation to larger models and higher-dimensional text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V) generation. 5.1 Text-to-Image Generation Setup. We compare DiffusionART with Flow-GRPO, Flow-GRPO-Fast (CPS) [6,20], DanceGRPO [9], FlowDPPO [18], and DiffusionNFT [7] with and without EMA, denoted DiffusionNFT (EMA) and DiffusionNFT (on-policy). All methods train LoRA adapters [21] with rank = 32 and scaling factor α = 64 at 512 512 resolution, without CFG or reference-policy KL regularization. On SD3.5-M, we use learning rate of 3 104 and 10-step rollouts. DiffusionNFT uses the original per-task hyperparameters [7] to maximize its baseline performance. Singleand multi-reward optimization. We evaluate SD3.5-M [22] on GenEval [23], OCR, and PickScore [19], and further jointly optimize GenEval, PickScore, CLIPScore [24], and HPSv2.1 [25]. Figure 5(ad) shows that DiffusionART behaves similarly under singleand multi-reward training. Figure 5(d) plots the total reward, with components in Appendix A.4. Without per-task EMA tuning, DiffusionART avoids the severe collapse of DiffusionNFT (on-policy) and achieves training efficiency comparable to DiffusionNFT (EMA). It is also much faster than Flow-GRPO, reaching Flow-GRPOs step-500 reward with 10.0, 5.2, and 9.6 fewer training steps on GenEval, OCR, and PickScore, respectively. Figure 5: Training rewards: (ac) singleand (d) multi-reward SD3.5-M. Scaling to larger models. We extend the same recipe to FLUX.1-dev (12B) [26] on GenEval, using six-step rollouts and its built-in guidance embedding at scale 3.5, without additional CFG. For DiffusionNFT, we retain β = 1 and rollout-policy EMA decay min(0.001n, 0.5) from the SD3.5-M GenEval baseline, where counts successful training updates. As shown in Figure 6(a), DiffusionART learns fastest among all methods, while DiffusionNFT exhibits pronounced training-reward fluctuations because these hyperparameters are not retuned for FLUX. Table 2 in Appendix A.1 reports the GenEval evaluation scores of different methods at step 500. Figure 6: (a) FLUX.1-dev on GenEval. (b) Guidance and restoration ablation on OCR. 8 Ablation of guidance and restoration. Figure 6(b) compares ART: 1 update and ART: 2 updates, two DiffusionART variants with the same covariance guidance, against NFT: 2 updates with carefully tuned β = 0.1. As explained in Appendix B.3, ART: 1 update learns quickly but gradually deteriorates. The second update in ART: 2 updates introduces restoration and provides long-term stability. In contrast, NFT: 2 updates briefly collapses to near zero before recovering. These results highlight the importance of both guidance type and restoration. 5.2 Text-to-Video Generation Setup. We fine-tune all parameters of the CFG-distilled HunyuanVideo-13B model [27] with learning rate of 105 and no KL regularization. Each group-based rollout uses 32 prompts and 8 videos per prompt. We generate 53-frame videos at 480 480 and 8 FPS with 16 sampling steps. VideoReward [28] scores videos at 4 FPS for training and evaluation. All methods use matched TA:VQ:MQ weights of 7:2:1 to improve output quality while preserving prompt following. Figure 7(ac) compares all three rewards over 400 training steps; Appendix A.5 reports an additional VQ:MQ = 1:1 comparison. Performance. As shown in Figure 7, DiffusionART surpasses all baselines in both VQ and MQ while keeping TA comparable with the strongest baseline. DiffusionART reaches training VQ of 6 and MQ of 3 after 29 and 46 steps, respectively; Flow-GRPO-Fast, DanceGRPO, and DiffusionNFT (EMA) do not reach these levels within their recorded trajectories. For VQ of 5.5, DiffusionART needs 24 steps and 63.4 GPU hours, versus 273 steps and 1,401.4 GPU hours for DiffusionNFT (EMA): 11.4 fewer training steps and 22.1 fewer GPU hours. It retains its gains through 400 steps and achieves evaluation VQ and MQ of 8.970 and 4.224, as reported in Table 3. DiffusionART improves evaluation VQ and MQ by 31.4% and 57.4%, respectively, over the strongest baseline. Figure 7: Efficient reward improvement across video generation. (ac) T2V: DiffusionART improves VQ and MQ fastest while maintaining TA comparable to the strongest baseline. (de) I2V: DiffusionART rapidly improves both rewards, whereas the baselines improve slowly or plateau. Ablation of trust-region masking. We remove only the trust-region mask described in Section 4.3, retaining normalized covariance guidance, timestep weighting, and two disjoint MSE updates. With VQ:MQ = 1:1 weights, Figure 8 shows that the no-mask run drops around step 200 before recovering, whereas the masked run improves steadily. Masking helps limit excessive updates, serving as an additional stability safeguard; Appendix A.7 provides further diagnostics of gradients and velocity drift, and Appendix A.6 reports the trust-region ablation on T2I tasks. Pairwise feedback and ablation of group size. The performance of DiffusionART with pairwise train reward is close to that obtained with scalar feedback, using scalar reward as the ground truth evaluation metric. Meanwhile, DiffusionART is insensitive to the group size K, and smaller substantially reduces GPU hours. Table 1 shows that, under the same 400-step budget with pairwise feedback, = 2 reaches final VQ of 12.235, no lower than 12.092 for = 8. Because = 2 uses only quarter of the rollout videos and training samples, it consumes only 260.8 GPU hours over the 400 steps, 3.4 fewer than the 883.3 GPU hours of = 8. One pair per prompt thus suffices for stable and compute-efficient optimization in this setting. 9 Table 1: VQ-only evaluation and GPU hours at step 400. Method GPU Hours VQ Scalar, = 8 Pairwise, = 2 Pairwise, = 4 Pairwise, = 8 891.1 13.637 260.8 12.235 465.6 10.883 883.3 12.092 Figure 8: T2V with and without trust-region masking. 5.3 Image-to-Video Generation Setup. We fine-tune all parameters of the CFGand step-distilled Wan2.1-I2V-14B model [29] released by LightX2V [30]. Each rollout uses 32 prompts, FLUX.1-dev reference images, and 8 videos per prompt. We generate 53-frame videos at 400 640 and 8 FPS with four sampling steps. All methods use VQ:MQ = 1:1 weights, learning rate of 105, and no KL regularization. Reward-model settings follow Section 5.2. Performance. DiffusionART improves both VQ and MQ efficiently, whereas the baselines improve slowly or plateau (Figure 7(de)). It reaches MQ of 6 in 45.8 GPU hours versus 220.3 for Flow-GRPO-Fast, 4.8 reduction. DiffusionNFT plateaus early and remains near that plateau through 400 updates, which we attribute to the residual self-consistency force diluting reward-improving guidance after gradient aggregation. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied why NFT-style forward-process diffusion post-training can be unstable and found that its objective can introduce an implicit forwardreverse self-consistency force that is not reliably canceled across states, while stronger restoration can improve stability at the cost of slower reward optimization. DiffusionART presents simple but effective way to systematically cancel the unstable force by aggregating endpoint reward guidance before assigning it to reverse-rollout states, and then using second update with trust-region mechanism to provide drift-adaptive restoration for stabilization. Experiments on image and video generation show efficient, stable reward improvement, including with pairwise feedback and small rollout groups. Beyond the algorithm, our work provides insights into forward-process training, offering clearer understanding of diffusion reinforcement learning and path toward scalable diffusion post-training for visual generation.

A.5 Alternative Reward Weights for T2V Figure 10 compares all methods with VQ:MQ = 1:1 weights and no TA reward. DiffusionART reaches training VQ of 6 in 20 steps, compared with 50 for DiffusionNFT (EMA) and 427 for Flow-GRPO-Fast: 2.5 and 21.4 fewer training steps. It uses 44.2 GPU hours, versus 250.2 and 502.5, giving 5.7 and 11.4 GPU-hour speedups. DanceGRPO reaches this level after 821 steps and 1805.5 GPU hours. Using the mean raw VQ/MQ reward, (VQ + MQ)/2, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage reward levels of DiffusionNFT (EMA) and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 fewer GPU hours, respectively (Figure 1). Its mean reward over the final 50 training steps is 13.018, compared with 10.105 and 8.510 for the two baselines, representing improvements of 28.8% and 53.0%. For MQ of 3, DiffusionART needs 19 steps and 42.9 GPU hours, compared with 33 steps and 165.6 GPU hours for NFT, and 117 steps and 149.4 GPU hours for Fast. This gives 1.7/6.2 step speedups and 3.9/3.5 GPU-hour speedups over NFT/Fast. On the three SD3.5-M benchmarks and FLUX.1-dev, training remains effective without masking and can improve slightly faster (Figure 12). On FLUX.1-dev, the no-mask run reaches training GenEval score of 0.971 by step 180. The benefit of masking is more pronounced for video generation (Figure 8); Appendix A.7 examines its stabilizing effect beyond reward curves. Figure 12: Image trust-region mask ablation. (ac) SD3.5-M; (d) FLUX.1-dev. A.7 Trust-Region Masking Diagnostics We further inspect the matched HunyuanVideo comparison with VQ:MQ weights of 1:1. Without masking, training exhibits larger late-stage gradient and velocity-drift spikes (Figure 13), complementing the reward curves in Figure 8(ab). Although the mask constrains only the second update of each rollout, its stabilizing effect extends to subsequent first updates. Over the shared first 300 training steps, the maximum first-update gradient norm is 1.96 with masking, compared with 3.33 without it. The velocity drift measured before second updates, which reflects displacement caused by the first update, also shows much larger spikes without masking (Figure 13). With masking, the velocity drift score stays healthy level. These observations suggest that restricting second updates helps keep later first updates well behaved, rather than merely suppressing gradients at the masked update. Figure 13: Trust-region diagnostics on HunyuanVideo-13B. (a) Parameter gradient norm before clipping. (b) Scheduler-reference-weighted velocity drift energy, averaged over training states before each update.

The coefficient 1 2K doesnt matter since the covariance will be normalized to form the guidance. Guidance assignment. We compare prompt-global and pairlocal guidance on GenEval, using 24 images per prompt to form 12 disjoint pairs. Prompt-global guidance aggregates pair covariances before normalization and applies the shared direction to all trajectories. Pair-local guidance normalizes each pairs covariance separately and applies it only to that pair. At step 400, prompt-global guidance reaches held-out GenEval score of 0.91, versus 0.78 for pair-local guidance. It also achieves higher training rewards (Figure 14), showing that the better practice is pooling the pairs of the same prompt together before computing the covariance to reduce the variance. Figure 14: Guidance assignment on GenEval. Rollout Stage Algorithm 2 DiffusionART-Pairwise: one training iteration 1: Sample with an ODE solver using v(0) θ = vθ. For each prompt c, collect an even number of endpoints x(i) 0 , states st, and predictions v(0) θ (st). 2: Form = K/2 disjoint pairs per prompt; query the pairwise reward model. 3: Assign pairwise rewards yi = 1 to winners, yi = 0 to losers, and yi = 1 4: Compute covariance guidance by Equation 5, replacing scalar rewards Ri with pairwise rewards yi. 5: Freeze vtgt(st) = v(0) θ (st) + G(c) for each state. 2 for ties. 6: Split the samples into two equal-sized disjoint minibatches B1, B2. 7: For each {B1, B2}, recompute w(st) and update θ with one step on Training Stage L(B; θ) = 1 (cid:80) stB w(st) MSE(vθ(st), vtgt(st)).
